paras: The Waterloo "all-white city" report was a widely published account, in late August and September 1903, that the citizens of Waterloo, Iowa, had ordered the town's Black residents to leave and that nearly all had gone. The story grew out of a Waterloo newspaper campaign for keeping the town "perfectly white," but Waterloo's mayor and local press denied that anyone had been driven out. Northern papers condemned the reported expulsion, while Southern papers cited it as proof that the North treated Black people no better than the South.

Before Aug. 27 the Waterloo Courier ran an editorial urging that a Black settlement in the city be discouraged, citing recent baseball games against Black teams as an "advertisement for others to come." The Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican quoted the Courier's plea to "keep perfectly white" and warned that "it is but a step from 'discouragement' of immigration to forced emigration."

A special dispatch from Waterloo dated Aug. 31 reported that "An All White City" was the town's motto and that the Black residents, "numbering a dozen families or so," had been "quietly notified that their presence was no longer desired." The correspondent traced the "climax" to visiting Black baseball teams whose players, he wrote, "assumed an air of equality" and drew the attention of "young white girls." One of the city's daily papers then began a "crusade," advising Black residents that "a quiet departure would save the adoption of harsh measures for their removal."

The dispatch stated that no violence was used or threatened but that an exodus began within a week. A shorter Waterloo dispatch of Sept. 2 said "the edict has gone forth that no negroes are wanted here" and that only two or three Black people remained. The Times-Republican reported the same day that Waterloo papers described an exodus following notice served editorially by the Courier and the Times-Tribune.

On Sept. 3 a Waterloo citizen wrote to Wm. Coalson of Des Moines that "there is nothing in the report," blaming "blooming idiots" and the visit of the Chicago Giant baseball club. A Waterloo editorial denied that any edict had come "from any recognized authority," blamed an anonymous correspondent, and conceded only "ill-considered editorial comment in some of the city papers."

Mayor P. J. Martin, answering a Washington correspondent who had sent him a Washington Post clipping, wrote that there was "not a word of truth" in it, that Waterloo had never had more than twenty-five Black residents, and that the story was the work of "an overzealous newspaper correspondent." In Des Moines, the Waterloo announcement largely prompted a Political Equality club discussion on Sept. 4 that ended in resolutions denouncing lynching.

The Aug. 31 dispatch ran in the Minneapolis Journal under "Waterloo Will Not Have Them," in the Saint Paul Globe under "Iowa Town Drives Away the Entire Negro Population," and in the Missouri Valley Times by Sept. 3. The Minneapolis Journal called it "whitecappery" and an "unlawful, unjust and cruel program," an editorial the Marshalltown paper reprinted.

Southern and Democratic papers took the story as a rebuke to the North. The Savannah Morning News, reprinted in Montgomery, wrote that residents were told to leave "if they value their lives and limbs," and the Raleigh News & Observer said "such a thing could not have occurred in any Southern town." The Irish Standard of Minneapolis said the residents left "under threats of personal violence," and Champ Clark's column in an Iowa Democratic paper attacked the "Republican negro haters of Waterloo."

The only Black paper found to cover the story, the Iowa State Bystander of Des Moines, did not report the expulsion as news. On Sept. 11 it printed the Waterloo denials as proof of how "dishonest some of our newspaper correspondents" were on the race question.

Accounts also disagree on threats: the Minneapolis Journal said "No threats were made," yet its own correspondent quoted a warning of "harsh measures," and distant editorials spoke of threats to life and limb. The denials came from the mayor and Waterloo's own press, while the Marshalltown report that Waterloo papers described an exodus, and the Waterloo editorial's admission of "ill-considered" comment, confirm at least a local press campaign against Black residents.

reader.title: Waterloo "all-white city" report
bases: The papers reported that Waterloo's Black residents were notified to leave and departed after a local newspaper campaign for an 'all-white' town (A2, A3, A9), though Waterloo's mayor and press denied any expulsion took place (A17, A19, A20).

The newspaper campaign to keep Waterloo 'perfectly white' is attested by several sources (A1, A3, A7, A17), but the reported notice and exodus rest on Waterloo correspondents' dispatches (A2, A9) and were flatly denied by the mayor, a Waterloo citizen and a Waterloo editorial (A16, A17, A19, A20).

framing.detail: The Waterloo dispatch ran under headlines such as 'Waterloo Will Not Have Them', 'Iowa Town Drives Away the Entire Negro Population' and 'Colored People Warned', with the correspondent's account of Black ball players' 'air of equality'.
The Minneapolis Journal called the action 'unlawful, unjust and cruel' and 'whitecappery'; the Marshalltown Times-Republican called the Courier's proposal 'the forerunner of riot'.
Southern and Democratic papers (Savannah, Montgomery, Raleigh, the Irish Standard, Champ Clark's column) reported the expulsion as fact to argue that the North was no better than the South.
The Iowa State Bystander, the only Black paper found, did not report the expulsion as news but printed Waterloo's denials under 'That Waterloo Affair', calling the correspondents dishonest.

conflicts.note: The denials come from the mayor and Waterloo's own press and citizens, who had an interest in the town's reputation; the dispatch came from an unnamed local correspondent. The Times-Republican's report that Waterloo papers themselves described an exodus (A7) and the Waterloo editorial's admission of 'ill-considered editorial comment' (A17) support the newspaper campaign but not the scale of the exodus.

record_check.dossier: Contested: the dispatch's account of a notified and departed Black population was denied by the mayor and Waterloo's press; only the newspaper campaign is corroborated.
Late August 1903 (Courier editorial before Aug. 27; dispatch Aug. 31 says the exodus followed within a week of the 'edict').
No mob is reported; the notice came through local newspapers' editorials and unnamed 'conservative citizens'.
ordered_out (by editorial notice) is reported but denied; the threat is contested: the dispatch says none was made but quotes a warning of 'harsh measures'.
Unnamed Black residents, 'a dozen families or so' per the dispatch; no more than twenty-five per the mayor.

record_check.record: Club women's denunciation as the cause; no further facts about the order
record_check.dossier: The papers give a full account of the reported order (Courier editorials, baseball visit, exodus) and of Waterloo's denials; the Des Moines club meeting was a response to it.
1903-08-27 (Marshalltown Times-Republican on the Courier editorial); the dispatch ran Aug. 31.
Coverage is fuller than the tier suggests: a long local dispatch, local Iowa commentary, and the mayor's denial.

info: Late August 1903: a Waterloo Courier editorial urging Black settlement be discouraged appeared before Aug. 27; the Aug. 31 dispatch said the 'reform' began a few weeks earlier and the exodus followed within a week of the 'edict'.
Waterloo's Black residents, described as 'a dozen families or so' (Aug. 31 dispatch); the mayor said there had never been more than twenty-five Black residents.

No crime was alleged; the stated reasons were the growth of the Black population, Black baseball teams' 'air of equality' and attention from 'young white girls', and the claim that 'the lawless type' would follow.
Unnamed 'conservative citizens' and one or more Waterloo daily papers; the Courier and Times-Tribune are named as having served notice editorially.
None reported; the Savannah News noted there had been 'no assault and no lynching'.
